strengths: The paper addresses a significant problem in camera-controllable video/world generation: maintaining spatial consistency over long horizons when revisiting previously seen regions. The critique of globally fused 3D memory accumulating pose/depth misalignment is well motivated and relevant to current memory-augmented video generation methods.

The core idea of storing per-frame local point-cloud memories, retrieving a coverage-maximizing subset for a target trajectory, and learning to reconcile multiple rendered anchors is technically sensible and reasonably original. It is a clear alternative to global 3D fusion rather than just an incremental conditioning tweak.

The method is described coherently. The coverage-driven retrieval formulation, anchor-video construction, shared multi-anchor attention, and pose-guided fusion are easy to follow, and the figures communicate the design well.

The experimental section compares against a broad set of relevant camera-control and memory-based baselines, including ViewCrafter, Gen3C, TrajCrafter, EPiC, SEVA, Context-as-Memory, and SPMem. Results on RealEstate10K and DL3DV show consistent gains in PSNR/SSIM and VBench-style quality metrics.

The ablations support the main design choices: local memories outperform global point-cloud conditioning, more retrieved anchors improve consistency, and qualitative analyses illustrate the benefits of pose-guided fusion and joint attention.
The approach is practical in that it freezes large video backbones and trains only the added controller, and it is demonstrated on two different DiT-based backbones, suggesting some generality.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still somewhat narrow relative to the claims of scalable long-horizon world consistency. The main quantitative setting is a partial-revisit reconstruction protocol on 500 sampled videos, while the more ambitious open-domain, keyboard-controlled, 241-frame generation results are mostly qualitative.

The metrics are imperfect for the stated goal. PSNR/SSIM against ground truth and VBench dimensions do not fully measure 3D spatial consistency, revisit correctness, or camera-following over long horizons. The paper would be stronger with explicit pose/camera tracking metrics in the main evaluation, loop-closure consistency, 3D reprojection consistency, or human preference studies.

Several strong baselines are reimplemented because they are not open-sourced, but the paper provides limited evidence that these reimplementations match the original methods' expected performance. This makes some comparisons, especially to Context-as-Memory and SPMem, harder to interpret.

The method depends heavily on external 3D reconstruction quality from TTT3R and estimated camera poses. Failure cases under dynamic objects, low-texture scenes, reflective surfaces, inaccurate poses, or severe occlusion are not analyzed in sufficient depth, even though these are central risks for local point-cloud memory.

The ablation of global versus local memory is compelling but somewhat coarse: the global-memory baseline may be disadvantaged by using a single rendered anchor, while the proposed local-memory version also benefits from multiple anchors and learned fusion. A more controlled comparison between global multi-rendering, local single-anchor, and local multi-anchor variants would isolate the source of improvement better.

The retrieval strategy is greedy and intuitive, but its computational cost, memory growth over arbitrarily long videos, and scalability with dense histories are not quantified. Long-horizon generation may become expensive as the memory bank grows.

The paper contains small reproducibility and consistency issues, such as different stated denoising application ranges between the main text and appendix, limited low-level details on pose normalization/rendering choices, and no clear discussion of code/model release, licensing, or runtime requirements.
The limitations and societal-impact discussion are minimal. For a generative video method, possible misuse, hallucination risks, dataset bias, and failure modes deserve more explicit treatment.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: long-horizon, camera-controllable video generation with spatial consistency when revisiting previously seen regions.

The central idea of avoiding a single fused global point cloud and instead retrieving multiple local geometric memories is sensible and well motivated by known pose/depth misalignment issues in long-horizon 3D reconstruction.

The method is described at a reasonably high level, with clear components: local memory construction, coverage-driven retrieval, multi-anchor attention, pose-guided fusion, and iterative memory update.
The paper compares against several relevant camera-control and memory-augmented baselines, and includes ablations for local versus global memory, number of retrieved anchors, and controller design.

Quantitative results show consistent gains in PSNR/SSIM and modest quality improvements over baselines on the stated partial-revisit benchmark, and the qualitative figures generally support the claim that multi-anchor conditioning can reduce visible drift.
weaknesses: The main experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. The core claim is long-horizon world consistency, but the primary quantitative evaluation is a 49-frame partial-revisit reconstruction setup using held-out frames from RealEstate10K/DL3DV. This is a useful proxy, but it does not adequately validate arbitrarily long exploration, open-domain generalization, 360-degree revisits, or dynamic/game-like settings, which are mostly shown qualitatively.

The novelty appears incremental. The method combines existing ingredients: per-frame point clouds from a pretrained reconstructor, greedy coverage retrieval, rendered anchor conditioning, ControlNet-style injection, attention over multiple anchors, and pose-guided weighting. The paper does not make a strong case that the algorithmic contribution is fundamentally new beyond a plausible engineering recombination of known ideas.

Baseline fairness is hard to assess. Important memory baselines such as Context-as-Memory and SPMem are reimplemented because they are not open sourced, but the paper gives limited evidence that these reimplementations are faithful or competitive. Some baselines are adapted to use the authors' retrieval strategy with K=1, which may not reflect their intended operating regime.

The evaluation mixes backbone effects and method effects. AnchorWeave is reported with both CogVideoX and Wan2.2, while several reimplemented baselines use CogVideoX only. Although a CogVideoX version of AnchorWeave is included, the presentation emphasizes best overall results, making it less clean to isolate the contribution of the proposed memory design.

The ablations are incomplete. The global-vs-local memory ablation compares a single global anchor against multiple local anchors, so it conflates memory representation with number of conditioning signals. The pose-guided fusion and joint-attention ablations are primarily qualitative, without quantitative metrics showing their individual impact.

Several implementation details needed for reproducibility are underspecified, including the exact FoV overlap threshold, coverage computation, point rendering parameters, occlusion handling, memory-bank growth/pruning strategy, and how generated-frame geometry errors accumulate over long horizons.

The paper relies heavily on pretrained 3D reconstruction and large video backbones, but does not analyze failure modes when TTT3R poses/depths are wrong, when dynamic objects dominate the scene, or when local memories disagree strongly. These are central to the claimed robustness of local-memory conditioning.

The long-horizon and open-domain claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper shows selected qualitative examples but provides no systematic user study, automated revisit-consistency metric, trajectory-following metric over long rollouts, or comparison under identical open-domain trajectories.

There are presentation and rigor issues: Table 4 duplicates TrajCrafter, appendix and main text disagree on whether the controller is applied during the first 80% or 90% of denoising steps, and the manuscript lacks a meaningful limitations or societal-impact discussion.

Overall, while the idea is plausible and the results are not without merit, the paper does not yet provide sufficiently rigorous or clean evidence for its broad claims. I would lean rejection unless the authors substantially strengthen the evaluation, clarify baseline fidelity, and disentangle the actual contribution of each component.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in long-horizon, camera-controllable video generation: maintaining spatial consistency when revisiting prior regions. The proposed shift from a single fused global 3D memory to multiple local geometric memories is well motivated and technically plausible, since it directly targets accumulated pose/depth fusion errors that can corrupt global point clouds.

AnchorWeave is a coherent system contribution. The coverage-driven memory retrieval, local point-cloud anchor rendering, shared multi-anchor attention, pose-guided fusion, and iterative update-retrieve-generate loop fit together naturally and are explained clearly enough to understand the design.

The experimental evidence is fairly strong. The paper compares against several relevant camera-control and memory-augmented baselines, reports both reconstruction/consistency metrics and VBench-style perceptual metrics, and evaluates with two large DiT backbones. The results show consistent gains in PSNR/SSIM and competitive or improved perceptual quality.

The ablations support the main claims: local memories outperform global point-cloud conditioning by a large margin, increasing the number of retrieved anchors improves consistency, and qualitative ablations make the roles of pose-guided fusion and shared attention intuitive.

The method appears practically relevant for interactive world models and long-horizon scene exploration, and the open-domain qualitative examples suggest promising generalization beyond the partial-revisit benchmark.
weaknesses: The main quantitative benchmark is a partial-revisit setting with ground-truth frames, which is useful but does not fully validate the more ambitious claims about open-ended long-horizon world generation. The strongest long-horizon and free-form trajectory evidence is largely qualitative.

The evaluation relies heavily on PSNR/SSIM and generic VBench dimensions. These do not directly measure 3D spatial consistency, revisit fidelity, camera-path adherence over long horizons, or accumulated drift; a more targeted geometric consistency metric or user study would strengthen the case.

Some important baselines, including Context-as-Memory and SPMem, are reimplemented because they are not open-sourced. Although the authors attempt fairness, the paper would benefit from more detail or validation showing that these reimplementations are competitive with the original methods.

The method depends on pretrained 3D reconstruction/pose estimation quality, especially TTT3R. The paper argues local memories reduce fusion artifacts, but failure modes under poor depth, reflective/textureless regions, dynamic objects, or inaccurate poses are not sufficiently analyzed.

The computational and memory costs of storing per-frame local point clouds, retrieving over a growing memory bank, rendering multiple anchors, and adding controller modules are not quantified. This matters for the claimed interactive/long-horizon use case.

A few implementation details are inconsistent or underspecified, such as applying the controller during the first 90% of denoising steps in the main text versus 80% in the appendix. The retrieval algorithm also omits some thresholds and practical details needed for full reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: maintaining spatial consistency in long-horizon, camera-controllable video generation. The diagnosis that globally fused 3D memories accumulate pose/depth misalignment is convincing and well motivated.

AnchorWeave proposes a coherent alternative: per-frame local geometric memories, coverage-driven retrieval, and a multi-anchor controller with shared anchor attention and pose-guided fusion. The components fit the problem well and the overall system is technically plausible.

Experimental results are broad for this topic. The paper compares against several strong camera-control and memory-augmented baselines on RealEstate10K and DL3DV, reports both fidelity/consistency and perceptual metrics, and evaluates two video backbones, CogVideoX and Wan2.2.

The quantitative gains are meaningful, especially against global-memory variants and SPMem-style baselines. The local-vs-global memory ablation is particularly supportive, showing a large PSNR/SSIM improvement when replacing global point clouds with local point clouds.

The appendix strengthens the submission with implementation details, retrieval pseudocode, camera controllability metrics, long-horizon stress tests, efficiency scaling, dynamic-content discussion, and explicit failure cases such as reflective surfaces and pose drift.

The method has potential impact for interactive world models, scene exploration, and long-form video generation because it addresses a practical failure mode of 3D-memory conditioning rather than only improving short-clip quality.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental at the system level. The paper combines known ingredients: local point-cloud renderings, greedy coverage retrieval, ControlNet-style conditioning, cross-anchor attention, and pose-conditioned weighting. The contribution is valuable, but the algorithmic novelty is not as strong as the empirical system result.

Some key ablations are qualitative or incomplete. Pose-guided fusion and shared-vs-separate attention are primarily demonstrated visually; quantitative ablations for these modules, retrieval strategy variants, number/location of control layers, and robustness to poor pose/depth estimates would make the technical case stronger.

The evaluation setting is still somewhat narrow. The main quantitative protocol is a partial-revisit reconstruction task on datasets also used for training, with PSNR/SSIM against ground truth. This favors methods that reconstruct observed trajectories and may not fully capture open-ended world-model behavior under novel free-form trajectories.

Several baselines are reimplemented because they are not open-sourced. Although the authors make an effort to match data and training, the paper cannot fully rule out implementation or tuning differences, especially for SPMem and Context-as-Memory.

The long-horizon and open-domain claims rely heavily on qualitative examples and supplementary videos. The 2400-frame stress test is useful, but it is reported on only 20 initial images and mainly with revisit PSNR; broader quantitative measures of drift, geometry consistency, and user-perceived quality would better support the strongest claims.

The method remains computationally expensive: Wan2.2 inference at 81x480x832 takes 275 seconds and 39GB GPU memory for K=4. This limits interactive use despite the paper framing the work around controllable world exploration.

The method depends strongly on the quality of the 3D estimator and mostly assumes static geometry. Dynamic scenes require masking, and out-of-sight object state changes are deferred to future monitor-style modules, so the current solution is not yet a general dynamic-world memory model.

There are minor clarity and consistency issues: the main text says the controller is applied during the first 90% of denoising steps, while the appendix says 80%; Table 2 reports SSIM as 53.45/67.27 whereas other tables use 0.x formatting; and some training/evaluation details such as exact splits and baseline hyperparameter tuning are underspecified.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon, camera-controllable video generation. The motivation that globally fused point clouds accumulate pose/depth misalignment is plausible and relevant for current memory-augmented video models.

The proposed alternative of keeping per-frame local geometric memories, retrieving coverage-complementary anchors, and learning a multi-anchor fusion controller is coherent. The method is technically reasonable and aligns well with the stated failure mode of global 3D memory.

The manuscript includes several useful pieces of evidence beyond a single benchmark table: comparisons against camera-control and memory baselines, K=1 versus multi-anchor variants, global versus local memory, efficiency measurements, long-horizon qualitative examples, stress-test discussion, and failure-mode/limitation analysis.
The paper is generally readable, with figures that communicate the intended pipeline and the qualitative differences between global and local memory conditioning.
weaknesses: The main evaluation protocol is not fully convincing for the claimed long-horizon world-consistency contribution. The paper samples 70 frames, uses 49 as the target segment, and uses the remaining 21 as historical context for retrieval. This can turn the task into partial view reconstruction/interpolation from nearby held-out frames rather than true chronological long-horizon generation, especially because the method explicitly retrieves context frames that maximize target coverage.

Baseline fairness is a serious concern. Several key baselines are reimplemented because they are not open sourced, but there is little validation that these reimplementations match the original methods. Some baselines are adapted with the authors' retrieval strategy, while AnchorWeave is also evaluated with a stronger Wan2.2 backbone, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of the proposed memory mechanism.

The ablation evidence is incomplete. The global-versus-local comparison appears to compare a single global anchor against multiple local anchors, so it does not cleanly isolate memory representation from number of conditioning anchors. The pose-guided fusion and shared-attention components are mainly supported qualitatively, and there is no strong quantitative comparison against simpler retrieval strategies such as nearest-pose, top-K overlap, random candidates, or learned retrieval.

The claimed long-horizon capability is supported mostly by qualitative examples and a limited stress test against SPMem. There is no robust quantitative evaluation of autoregressive error accumulation, revisit consistency under strictly causal memory, or performance when generated frames rather than ground-truth frames dominate the memory bank.

The method remains heavily dependent on external 3D reconstruction and camera pose estimation, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze sensitivity to pose/depth noise, failure under poor reconstruction, or the cost/robustness tradeoff of TTT3R in realistic deployment.

Dynamic-scene handling is weak relative to the broad world-modeling framing. The method is essentially a static-scene memory system; dynamic examples require masking foreground characters, and out-of-sight dynamic state is deferred to future work.

Reproducibility is limited. Important implementation choices are scattered, some details appear inconsistent between main text and appendix, and the evidence relies partly on supplementary videos via an anonymized webpage. Without code, exact evaluation scripts, and validated baseline implementations, the empirical case is hard to verify.

Overall, the idea has merit, but the experimental design does not yet provide a sufficiently clean or convincing case for the strong claims about long-horizon world-consistent video generation. I would lean against acceptance unless the evaluation protocol and ablations are substantially strengthened.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in long-horizon, camera-controllable video generation: maintaining spatial consistency when revisiting previously observed regions. The central idea of replacing a brittle fused global 3D memory with multiple local per-frame geometric memories is well motivated and clearly connected to a real failure mode of prior memory-based methods.

The proposed system is technically coherent: coverage-driven retrieval selects complementary local memories, rendered anchors provide geometric conditioning, and the multi-anchor weaving controller combines shared cross-anchor attention with pose-guided fusion. These components fit together naturally and represent a meaningful algorithmic contribution rather than just an engineering variant.

The empirical evidence is fairly strong. AnchorWeave is compared against a broad set of recent camera-control and memory-augmented baselines, including ViewCrafter, Gen3C, TrajCrafter, EPiC, SEVA, Context-as-Memory, and SPMem. Quantitative results show consistent gains in PSNR/SSIM and VBench-style quality metrics, and the qualitative examples support the claimed improvements in revisit consistency.

The ablations support the main design choices: local point clouds outperform a global point cloud, increasing the number of retrieved anchors improves consistency, and the paper provides targeted analyses of global fusion degradation, runtime scaling, long-horizon stress tests, dynamic-content handling, and failure modes.

The paper is clearly written overall, with helpful diagrams explaining the retrieval and multi-anchor conditioning pipeline. The limitations section is substantive and appropriately acknowledges dependence on the video backbone, 3D reconstruction quality, static-memory assumptions, pose drift, reflective surfaces, and efficiency constraints.
weaknesses: Some key ablations are more qualitative than quantitative. In particular, pose-guided fusion and shared versus separate attention are mainly justified through visual examples; numerical ablations for these controller choices would make the scientific case stronger.

The evaluation setting is somewhat narrow relative to the broad long-horizon world-modeling claims. The main quantitative benchmark is a partial-revisit setup on RealEstate10K and DL3DV, while open-domain, 360-degree, third-person, and very long-horizon results are largely qualitative or diagnostic. This is acceptable for the contribution, but it leaves some uncertainty about robustness in diverse real-world interactive settings.

Several baselines are reimplemented because they are not open-sourced. The paper states that the same data and backbone are used where possible, but reimplementation details and possible performance gaps could materially affect the comparison, especially against Context-as-Memory and SPMem.

The method depends heavily on the quality of TTT3R pose/depth estimates and on the assumption that most useful scene memory is static. The paper discusses this, but the main experiments do not deeply quantify degradation under poor reconstruction, dynamic scenes, reflective materials, or accumulated generated-memory errors.

The computational cost is nontrivial: full multi-anchor generation increases runtime and memory over SPMem, and inference remains dominated by slow diffusion denoising. The quality-cost tradeoff is reported, but this may limit practical use in interactive applications unless accelerated.

Reproducibility would benefit from more precise details on train/test splits, retrieval thresholds, candidate filtering criteria, and exact metric protocols. The manuscript gives many implementation details, but some retrieval and evaluation choices remain underspecified enough to make independent reproduction challenging.
